title: World Cup Final Shatters Ticket Price Records as Average Seat Costs $11,327
excerpt: Argentina versus Spain at MetLife Stadium on Sunday is the most expensive sporting event in U.S. history, surpassing every Super Bowl on record.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • The 2026 World Cup final's average ticket price is $11,327, a U.S. record.
  • Cheapest resale tickets range from $7,448 to $8,269, with some at $30,000.
  • FIFA's resale marketplace lists tickets up to $2.3 million for Category 3 seats.
  • President Trump will attend the final amid a class-action lawsuit against FIFA.
  • The final surpasses previous records held by Super Bowls for ticket prices.

  • The 2026 World Cup final between Argentina and Spain at MetLife Stadium has an average ticket purchase price of $11,327, making it the most expensive sporting event in U.S. history.
  • The cheapest available tickets on secondary markets range from $7,448 to $8,269. FIFA's last-minute Category 1 seats are listed at $30,000 each.
  • On FIFA's official resale marketplace, individual listings reach as high as $575,000 for Category 1 and $2.3 million for a single Category 3 seat.
  • President Trump, who helped secure the 2026 tournament for North America, will attend Sunday's final. FIFA faces a class-action lawsuit over its ticket sales practices.

The Price of History

If Lionel Messi lifts the World Cup trophy on Sunday, the fans who watched him do it will have paid more for the privilege than anyone in the history of American sports.

The 2026 World Cup final between Argentina and Spain at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey, has broken every ticket-price record on file. According to TickPick, the average purchase price has reached $11,327, surpassing Super Bowl 58 between the Kansas City Chiefs and San Francisco 49ers ($9,411) as the most expensive sporting event in the United States.

Even getting in the door costs a fortune. As of Friday, the cheapest available tickets across major resale platforms ranged from $7,448 on SeatGeek to $8,269 on StubHub. FIFA's own last-minute sales portal still had Front Category 1 seats available — at $30,000 each.

"A class-action lawsuit alleges "deceptive" ticket sales practices, including seat-switching after purchase."

Six-Figure Seats and a Class-Action Suit

The extreme pricing extends well into six figures. On FIFA's official resale marketplace, listings soar as high as $575,000 for Category 1, $595,000 for Front Category 1 and an extraordinary $2.3 million for a single seat in Category 3. Whether those upper-end tickets actually sell is another matter, but they reflect the unprecedented demand surrounding what may be Messi's final World Cup match.

"This becomes sort of like the pinnacle of that sort of world event, that Mount Rushmore moment."

— Matt Ferrel, VP and head of growth, TickPick

FIFA's pricing strategy has drawn legal fire. A class-action lawsuit alleges "deceptive" ticket sales practices, including seat-switching after purchase. The attorneys general of New York and New Jersey have issued subpoenas over inflated prices and dynamic pricing tactics that saw some seats initially listed at $2 million.

Even President Trump, who helped secure the 2026 tournament for North America and plans to attend Sunday's final, called the prices excessive. "If people from Queens and Brooklyn and all of the people that love Donald Trump can't go, I would be disappointed," he told the New York Post.

The Most Expensive U.S. Sporting Events

The World Cup final now leads a list that was previously dominated by NFL championship games. Based on average purchase price, the five most expensive U.S. sporting events are:

  1. 2026 World Cup Final (Spain vs. Argentina): $11,327
  2. Super Bowl 58 (Chiefs vs. 49ers, 2024): $9,411
  3. Super Bowl 55 (Buccaneers vs. Chiefs, 2021): $7,313
  4. Super Bowl 54 (Chiefs vs. 49ers, 2020): $6,546
  5. 2026 NBA Finals Game 3 (Knicks vs. Spurs): $6,308

What's Driving the Demand

Multiple factors are converging to push prices to these levels. The match features two global powerhouses — Spain seeking its second World Cup title and Argentina defending its crown. It is almost certainly the last World Cup appearance for 39-year-old Messi, who could become just the fourth player in tournament history to win both the Golden Boot and Golden Ball in the same edition.

The venue adds to the spectacle. MetLife Stadium holds 82,500 fans, smaller than the expanded-format tournament's other showcase venues. And the New York metropolitan area offers a concentration of wealthy sports consumers unlike any other market.

For comparison, tickets to Argentina's semifinal victory over England had a get-in price of $3,177 at kickoff. Saturday's third-place match between France and England in Miami has a get-in price of just $653.

Sunday's final kicks off at 3 p.m. ET, concluding the largest World Cup in history — 48 teams across 16 cities over 39 days. The White House has confirmed that President Trump will be in attendance, adding a layer of security and ceremony to what is already the biggest single-day event in global sports.
